title: Bridal lace shawl
subtitle: A fan-lace rectangle in lace-weight yarn, with five-treble fans separated by picot chains, after Weldon's Practical Crochet
excerpt: This rectangular shawl measures 175 cm wide by 55 cm deep and is worked in lace-weight white or ivory yarn on a 2.75 mm hook. The pattern is a fan-lace repeat: five-treble fans separated by chain-space columns, with a three-chain picot at the centre of each fan. Adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet. Requires accurate lace counting and consistent fine-yarn tension.
sourceNotes: Adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 7 (1892), bridal and fine lace shawl chapter (Internet Archive, archive.org). Fan lace construction confirmed against Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).
heroPrompt: A delicate rectangular crochet shawl in ivory lace-weight yarn pinned out fully on a dark surface, photographed from directly above, showing the fan-lace pattern with picot points along the lower edge.

crochet.gaugeText: One fan repeat (5 tr + 2 chain columns) = approximately 2.5 cm wide; 8 fan rows = 10 cm deep in lace-weight yarn with a 2.75 mm hook, measured after blocking.
crochet.finishedSizeText: Approximately 175 cm wide x 55 cm deep, after wet blocking.

glossaryTerms.definition: A lace pattern where groups of trebles are worked into the same chain space to create a fan or shell shape, separated by chain columns and anchored with a dc on the return row. Each fan sits above a chain space and the chain spaces sit above each fan.
A short chain of three worked from the centre top of a fan, then fastened with a slip stitch to produce a decorative point. The picot adds height and decoration at the peak of each fan.

content.text: This rectangle is worked from one short end to the other in a
fan-lace
repeat of five trebles into a chain space, with a
picot chain

at the centre of each fan. The fabric is very open and relies entirely on blocking to lie flat and show its full width. Work in good light and count each fan carefully: the pattern repeat is 8 chains (plus 2 edge chains), so the foundation chain must be a multiple of 8 plus 4.

This is an advanced pattern due to the fine yarn, the small hook size, and the need to maintain consistent tension across a very wide foundation chain of over 400 stitches. Work a swatch of at least 40 chains and block it before starting the full piece to check both the fan gauge and how the lace opens after blocking.

attrs.title: Materials
attrs.body: Approximately 200 g lace-weight yarn in white or ivory. A 2.75 mm crochet hook (US C/2). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat. Rust-proof pins. Tape measure. A good light source is essential when working fine yarn.

content.text: Gauge

One fan repeat (5 tr + 2 chain columns each side) = approximately 2.5 cm wide; 8 fan rows = 10 cm deep, measured after blocking. Block the swatch fully before measuring: unblocked lace-weight fabric measures considerably narrower than its blocked state. The shawl requires approximately 70 fan repeats across the width.
Stitches used
chain (ch): UK and US shared.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
fan: 5 tr into the same chain space.
picot chain: ch 3, sl st into base of chain.
Pattern

The rectangle is worked flat in rows from one short end. The fan repeat is 8 chains wide. The foundation chain of 564 chains gives 70 fan repeats plus edge stitches, which at 2.5 cm per repeat equals 175 cm blocked width.
Foundation chain
Ch 564. (70 x 8 = 560 working chains, plus 4 for the edge and turning chain.) Take care not to twist the chain. Place a stitch marker every 80 chains to help count.
Row 1 (right side)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the first ch. *Ch 3. Skip 3 ch. 1 dc in next ch. Ch 3. Skip 3 ch. 1 dc in next ch*; repeat from * to * across. Turn. (141 dc, 140 ch-3 spaces)
Row 2 (fan row)

Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. *Ch 2. 5 tr in next ch-3 space (fan). After the 2nd tr of the fan, ch 3 and sl st back into the 2nd tr (picot at centre top of fan). Complete the remaining 3 tr of the fan. Ch 2. 1 dc in next dc. Ch 2. 1 dc in next dc*; repeat from * to * across. Turn. (70 fans, 70 picots)
Row 3 (arch row)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. *Ch 3. 1 dc in the ch-2 space between the fan and the next dc. Ch 3. 1 dc in next dc*; repeat from * to * across. Turn. (141 dc, 140 ch-3 spaces)
Rows 4 to approximately 44
Alternate Row 2 (fan row) and Row 3 (arch row). After approximately 44 rows (22 fan rows) the piece measures approximately 55 cm deep. End on an arch row. Fasten off.
Finishing

Fasten off and weave in all ends with care: lace-weight ends are very fine and must pass through at least four stitches in two directions to stay secure. Wet-block thoroughly: soak in cool water for at least 20 minutes to allow full saturation, then press out excess moisture in a towel without wringing. Pin out to 175 x 55 cm on a blocking mat, placing pins at each picot point along the lower edge for a defined scallop line. Leave until fully dry.
Care
Handwash in cool water with a gentle wool or silk wash (according to the yarn fibre). Handle very gently when wet. Lay flat to dry. Re-pin after washing to restore the full blocked dimensions.
What to try next

The same fan-lace structure works as a triangular shawl: start with a short foundation chain and increase by one fan repeat at each edge on every fan row. A wider fan of 7 tr instead of 5 gives a more pronounced scallop along the lower edge. In fingering weight on a 3.25 mm hook the same pattern produces a warmer shawl with a more visible lace structure.
